title.en: Gandhi's early satyagrahas, Rowlatt Act and Khilafat
From a railway platform to a nation

text.en: In 1893 a young lawyer was thrown out of a first class compartment at Pietermaritzburg station because he was Indian. Mohandas Gandhi decided to fight, and the weapon he forged there, satyagraha, would one day shake an empire.

Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi was born on 2 October 1869 at Porbandar in Gujarat, where his father Kaba Gandhi was Diwan.
He sailed to England in 1888, became a barrister in 1891, and went to South Africa in April 1893 to help a Gujarati firm in a law suit.
At Pietermaritzburg station he was physically thrown out of the first class compartment, his first taste of racial discrimination.
In South Africa he developed satyagraha, meaning devotion to the truth or truth-force, with peaceful marches and willing arrest against unjust laws.
Influenced by Tolstoy, Ruskin and Thoreau, he founded the Phoenix Settlement in 1905 and the Tolstoy Farm in 1910 as training grounds for satyagrahis.
The Smuts-Gandhi Agreement finally abolished the poll tax on indentured labourers.
Gandhi returned to India in 1915 and, on the advice of his political guru Gopal Krishna Gokhale, toured the country to understand the people.
In Champaran, Bihar, peasants under the tinkathia system had to grow indigo on three-twentieths of their land, and Rajkumar Shukla persuaded Gandhi to visit.
Gandhi defied a police order to leave, and the Lieutenant Governor formed a committee that ended the tinkathia system.
Success at Champaran, the Ahmedabad mill strike and the Kheda satyagraha, both in 1918, made him a leader of mass struggle.
The Rowlatt Act allowed arrest without warrant and detention without trial, so Gandhi called it the Black Act and called a nation-wide satyagraha on 6 April 1919.
On 13 April 1919, General Dyer blocked the only exit of Jallianwala Bagh and fired for ten minutes, killing 379 by the official count.
Tagore returned his knighthood and Gandhi surrendered his Kaiser-i-Hind medal in protest.
The Khilafat Movement, led by the Ali brothers, gave Gandhi a chance to unite Hindus and Muslims, and the Khilafat Committee adopted non-cooperation on 9 June 1920.

problem.en: In which three satyagrahas did Gandhi first lead Indian peasants and workers?

text.en: Champaran in 1917 freed peasants from the tinkathia indigo system.

why.en: The planters took indigo on three-twentieths of the land.

text.en: Ahmedabad mill workers struck in 1918 and Gandhi guided them.
Kheda peasants refused revenue in 1918 after crop failure.

why.en: Together these made Gandhi a mass leader.

prompt.en: Explain the Rowlatt Act and why Indians opposed it.

requiredIdeas.en: Arrest without warrant and detention without trial
Called the Black Act by Gandhi

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking the Rowlatt Act caused the Khilafat Movement

points.en: Rowlatt Act 1919 and Jallianwala Bagh, 13 April 1919.
Khilafat Movement led to non-cooperation in 1920.
